background.source: The American Presidential System is a form of government where the head of government is typically referred to as the president and is directly or indirectly elected by a group of citizens for a term of four years. This system is separate from the legislative branch and is responsible for leading the executive branch of the government. The president serves as both the head of government and head of state, unlike in a parliamentary system where the head of government is selected by gaining the confidence of an elected legislature. The presidential system originated from a time when the person presided over the governing body and in the early days of the United States where the President of the Continental Congress held such powers. This system is prevalent in the mainland Americas, Central and southern West Africa, and Central Asia. With elections happening every four years, the American Presidential System depends heavily on the democratic process to maintain its stability and progression.
background.target: The French Presidential System is a form of government that places the head of government, typically with the title of president, as the leader of an executive branch that operates separately from the legislative branch. The president is usually the head of state and is directly or indirectly elected by citizens for a term that typically lasts for seven years in France. Unlike in a parliamentary system, the president is not responsible to the legislature and can only be dismissed in exceptional circumstances. This type of government is prevalent in mainland Americas, Central and southern West Africa, and Central Asia, with only a few examples seen in Europe.
